guide.title: Bronx Park, the Bronx: The Zoo, the Garden and the River
guide.intro: Bronx Park covers 718 acres, the eighth-largest park in New York City, bounded by Southern Boulevard, Webster Avenue, Gun Hill Road, Bronx Park East and East 180th Street. Much of the land came to the city under the 1884 New Parks Act, from Fordham University and from the Lorillard family, who had run a snuff mill beside the Bronx River. The New York Botanical Garden, founded in 1891, holds 250 acres in the northern section; the Bronx Zoo opened across 265 acres to the south on November 8, 1899. The river runs two miles through the park, and a 35-acre Forever Wild preserve covers part of the northern end. Pelham Parkway lies east, West Farms south and Belmont west.

sections.heading: The 1884 Act, the Garden and the Zoo
sections.body:
The 1884 New Parks Act brought most of this ground into the city's hands, much of it from Fordham University and the rest from the Lorillard family, whose snuff mill stood beside the Bronx River. Fordham's Rose Hill campus, which had once spanned over 100 acres, was reduced by that transfer and is now described as immediately west of the Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden. A 138-plot cemetery was relocated in 1890 from what is now the Garden.

The Garden was founded by act of the New York State Legislature on April 28, 1891, with Cornelius Vanderbilt II, Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan among its principal officers and Nathaniel Lord Britton as secretary; Britton and his wife, Elizabeth Gertrude Britton, led the fundraising campaign, taking the Royal Botanic Gardens in London as their model. It was designated a National Historic Landmark on May 28, 1967. Its Enid A. Haupt Conservatory broke ground on January 3, 1899 and was completed in 1902, and it was designated a New York City Landmark on October 16, 1973.

The Zoo opened on November 8, 1899 with 843 animals in 22 exhibits, four years after the New York Zoological Society — now the Wildlife Conservation Society — was founded by members of the Boone and Crockett Club. William Temple Hornaday was its first director, for thirty years. The American Bison Society was founded in 1905, and in 1913 the zoo sent fourteen bison to Montana's National Bison Range and to Wind Cave National Park.

The Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden are at the eastern terminus of Fordham Road in Bronx Park. Lake Agassiz and Bronx Lake lie inside the park, along with waterfalls and ponds, and the Bronx River — about 24 miles long altogether — passes through the park, the Garden and the Zoo on its way south.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The Bronx Zoo's own transit page names the 2 train to Pelham Parkway for the Bronx River entrance, Gate B, walking west from the station, and separately lists the 2 or 5 to West Farms Square/East Tremont, East 180th Street or Pelham Parkway without tying any one of the three to a gate. The New York Botanical Garden's directions name the B, D and 4 to Bedford Park Boulevard, then the Bx25 or Bx26 east, or on foot down Bedford Park Boulevard to Southern Boulevard, for the Mosholu Entrance. The same page names the 2 to Allerton Avenue, then west on Allerton and south on Bronx Park East to Waring Avenue, for the East Gate, which the Garden says is pedestrian and daytime access only.

Metro-North's Botanical Garden station sits on the Harlem Line at 2999 Southern Boulevard in Bedford Park, just north of Southern Boulevard's intersection with Bedford Park Boulevard, and its own article describes it as adjacent to northern Bronx Park and the New York Botanical Garden. It has two high-level side platforms serving the Harlem Line's outer tracks and connects to the Bx25, Bx26, Bx41 and Bx41 SBS. The Garden names the same station for its Mosholu Entrance. The Zoo names a different one: the Harlem Line to Fordham station, then the Bx9 eastward to 183rd Street and Southern Boulevard.

For buses the Garden lists the Bx19, Bx12, Bx22, Bx9 and Bx17 for its Main Entrance at 2900 Southern Boulevard, and the Bx25, Bx26, Bx41 and Bx34 for the Mosholu Entrance at 2950 Southern Boulevard. The Zoo lists the Bx9 or Bx19 to 183rd Street and Southern Boulevard for its Southern Boulevard pedestrian entrance, Gate C, and the Bx12 or Bx22 to Fordham Road and Southern Boulevard for the same gate. The Q44 from Queens to 180th Street and Boston Road serves the Asia gate, Gate A, and the BxM11 express bus, which stops along Madison Avenue between 26th and 99th Streets in Manhattan, runs to the Bronx River entrance.

This page does not name a ferry landing for Bronx Park.

faq.question: How do I get to Bronx Park?
faq.answer: By subway, Metro-North or bus, and which one depends on which institution you are heading for. The New York Botanical Garden's directions name the B, D and 4 to Bedford Park Boulevard, then the Bx25 or Bx26 east, for the Mosholu Entrance, and the 2 to Allerton Avenue for the East Gate. The Bronx Zoo's transit page names the 2 to Pelham Parkway for its Bronx River entrance and also lists the 2 or 5 to West Farms Square/East Tremont, East 180th Street or Pelham Parkway. On Metro-North, the Harlem Line's Botanical Garden station at 2999 Southern Boulevard is described as adjacent to northern Bronx Park and the Garden; the Zoo instead names the Harlem Line to Fordham station and the Bx9 east. The buses named between the two institutions are the Bx9, Bx12, Bx17, Bx19, Bx22, Bx25, Bx26, Bx34, Bx41 and Bx41 SBS, plus the Q44 from Queens and the BxM11 express from Madison Avenue in Manhattan. This page does not name a ferry landing for Bronx Park.

faq.question: When did the Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Garden open?
faq.answer: The Garden came first on paper: it was founded by an act of the New York State Legislature on April 28, 1891, and occupies 250 acres in the park's northern section. The Zoo opened to the public on November 8, 1899, with 843 animals in 22 exhibits, across 265 acres in the southern section. Both were designated within the park the city had begun assembling under the 1884 New Parks Act.

faq.question: Can you visit the Lorillard Snuff Mill?
faq.answer: The mill stands on Snuff Mill Road inside the New York Botanical Garden's grounds, so it is reached through the Garden. Built about 1840 by the P. Lorillard Company, it is now the Lillian and Amy Goldman Stone Mill and holds staff offices and a catering facility for the Garden rather than an exhibit of its own. Its designations predate the Garden's: a New York City Landmark on April 19, 1966, a National Historic Landmark and a National Register listing on December 22, 1977.

places.name: Bronx Park
places.summary: A 718-acre city park, the eighth-largest in New York City, bounded by Southern Boulevard to the southwest, Webster Avenue to the northwest, Gun Hill Road to the north, Bronx Park East to the east and East 180th Street to the south. It holds the New York Botanical Garden in its northern section and the Bronx Zoo in its southern one.
places.history: Much of the land was acquired under the 1884 New Parks Act, from Fordham University and from the Lorillard family. The Bronx River runs two miles through the park, which also holds Lake Agassiz, Bronx Lake, waterfalls and ponds, and a 35-acre Forever Wild nature preserve in its northern section.

places.name: New York Botanical Garden
places.address: Southern and Bedford Park Boulevards, Bronx, NY
places.summary: A 250-acre botanical garden in the northern section of Bronx Park, founded by an act of the New York State Legislature on April 28, 1891. It was designated a National Historic Landmark on May 28, 1967 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places the same day, reference number 67000009.
places.history:
Cornelius Vanderbilt II, Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan were among the principal officers; Nathaniel Lord Britton served as secretary and led the fundraising campaign with his wife, Elizabeth Gertrude Britton, taking the Royal Botanic Gardens in London as the model.

The Enid A. Haupt Conservatory, designed by Lord & Burnham with William R. Cobb as primary designer in an Italian Renaissance style modelled on the Palm House at Kew and on Joseph Paxton's Crystal Palace, broke ground on January 3, 1899 and was completed in 1902 at a cost of $177,000, built by John R. Sheehan for the city's parks department. It forms a 512-foot "C" of eleven pavilions under a 90-foot Palm House dome. Renovations in 1935 and 1950 removed original decoration; the 1978 restoration led by Edward Larrabee Barnes moved it back toward the original design, paid for by Enid Annenberg Haupt's $5 million gift and $5 million maintenance endowment, and the conservatory was renamed for her that year. Beyer Blinder Belle carried out a further $25 million renovation between 1993 and 1997. It was designated a New York City Landmark on October 16, 1973.

The LuEsther T. Mertz Library was founded in 1899 and designed by Robert W. Gibson in a Renaissance Revival style; the building was completed in 1900. First called the Museum Building and then the Administration Building, it was renamed for LuEsther Mertz in the 1990s, was a contributing property to the 1967 National Historic Landmark designation, and was designated a New York City Landmark on March 24, 2009. It holds two copies of the Circa Instans, of about 1190 and about 1275.

Beatrix Jones Farrand designed the rose garden in 1916; it was renovated in 2007. Charles Tefft's Fountain of Life dates from 1905. The Thain Family Forest, 50 acres of old-growth woodland along the Bronx River, was first called Hemlock Grove and briefly the Native Forest; eastern hemlock was historically dominant there and declined in the early twentieth century under hemlock woolly adelgid and elongate hemlock scale. Britton called the site "the most precious natural possession of the city of New York," and John and Carmen Thain supported the 2011 restoration that removed invasive species and expanded native vegetation.

places.name: Bronx Zoo
places.summary: A 265-acre zoo in the southern section of Bronx Park, opened on November 8, 1899 with 843 animals in 22 exhibits. It is managed by the Wildlife Conservation Society, which is headquartered here, and accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums; as of 2010 it held about 4,000 animals of 650 species.
places.history:
The New York Zoological Society, later renamed the Wildlife Conservation Society, was founded in 1895 by members of the Boone and Crockett Club, principally Madison Grant and C. Grant LaFarge. William Temple Hornaday was the zoo's first director, serving thirty years.

The original permanent buildings are Heins & LaFarge's Beaux-Arts pavilions around a circular sea lion pool, known as Astor Court and designated a New York City Landmark on June 20, 2000 after an attempt in 1966 had failed. Paul Manship's Rainey Memorial Gates were dedicated in 1934 as a memorial to Paul James Rainey, designated a city landmark on January 11, 1967 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972. The Rockefeller Fountain was designated on February 20, 1968, and Zoo Center — built in 1908 as the Elephant House — in 2000.

The American Bison Society was founded in 1905, and in 1913 the zoo sent fourteen bison to Montana's National Bison Range and to Wind Cave National Park. The zoo was the first in the United States to exhibit shoebills and Komodo dragons, in 1926, and the first in North America to exhibit an okapi, in 1937; it held four thylacines between 1902 and 1919, the last dying on September 13, 1919.

Among the exhibits: Congo Gorilla Forest, 6.5 acres with a trail about a third of a mile long, opened in 1999 and had received 7 million visits by 2009; JungleWorld, built around the jungles of Asia, where the Wildlife Conservation Society works with the Madras Crocodile Bank Trust Center for Herpetology on gharial conservation; Himalayan Highlands, opened June 27, 1986; the Gelada Reserve, opened in 1990; Tiger Mountain, opened May 15, 2003; Madagascar!, opened June 20, 2008 in the former Lion House of 1903; and World of Darkness, opened in 1969, closed in 2009 and reopened on July 12, 2025.

places.name: Lorillard Snuff Mill
places.summary: A stone mill built about 1840 by the P. Lorillard Company beside the Bronx River, on Snuff Mill Road within the New York Botanical Garden's grounds. Its own article calls it the oldest existing tobacco manufacturing building in the United States. It is now the Lillian and Amy Goldman Stone Mill, holding staff offices and a catering facility for the Garden.
places.history: The Lorillard firm had moved its operations to this Bronx site in 1792 and abandoned the mill in 1870, when it went to Jersey City. Built of locally quarried schist rock, it was designated a New York City Landmark on April 19, 1966, made a National Historic Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 22, 1977, reference number 77000935, and added to the New York State Register on June 23, 1980. A renovation between 1952 and 1954 added a café, a patio and a meeting room, and a $10.5 million restoration was completed in 2010.

places.name: Bronx River Forest
places.summary: A natural area along the Bronx River corridor whose southern extent reaches into the New York Botanical Garden. The Bronx River Alliance describes it as a remnant of the original forests and floodplains that once blanketed the corridor, holding many trees more than a hundred years old, and names upgraded paths, nature trails, boardwalks and overlooks.
places.history: It is managed by the Bronx River Alliance in partnership with the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation and, by the Alliance's own account, more than a hundred partner organizations. Recent work has focused on floodplain restoration, habitat expansion and public-access infrastructure.

entries.name: Bronx Park
entries.note: 718 acres between Southern Boulevard and Bronx Park East, with the Bronx River running two miles through the middle of it.

entries.name: New York Botanical Garden
entries.note: 250 acres in the park's northern section, founded April 28, 1891 and a National Historic Landmark since May 28, 1967.

entries.name: Bronx Zoo
entries.note: 2300 Southern Boulevard. Opened November 8, 1899 with 843 animals in 22 exhibits; now the Wildlife Conservation Society's headquarters.

entries.name: Lorillard Snuff Mill
entries.note: Built about 1840 on Snuff Mill Road, designated a New York City Landmark on April 19, 1966 and a National Historic Landmark in 1977.

entries.name: Bronx River Forest
entries.note: Paths, boardwalks and overlooks along the Bronx River corridor, managed by the Bronx River Alliance with NYC Parks.

links.note: Belmont's own article gives Bronx Park as its eastern boundary, and its Italian immigrants found work building the Zoo and the Garden from 1898.
Fordham Road runs west-east from the Harlem River to Bronx Park; the Zoo and the Garden are at its eastern terminus.
The Wildlife Conservation Society is headquartered at the Bronx Zoo and also runs the New York Aquarium, on Surf Avenue in Coney Island.
